title: Liaison
subtitle: Linking the final consonant of one word to the initial vowel of the next. Obligatory, forbidden, and optional liaisons.
objectives: Understand liaison as the linking of a silent final consonant to a following vowel.
Distinguish between obligatory, forbidden, and optional liaisons.
Pronounce common liaisons correctly: les amis [lez‿ami].
Recognize that liaison changes the sound of some consonants: s and x become [z].

sections.heading: What liaison is
sections.body:
Liaison is the linking of a word-final consonant to the initial vowel of the next word. The consonant is silent when the next word starts with a consonant, but pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel or silent h.

Consider 'les'. Before a consonant, it is [le]: les maisons. Before a vowel, it is [lez]: les amis. The s, silent in isolation, becomes [z] in liaison.

Liaison is not optional everywhere. Some liaisons are obligatory, some are forbidden, and some are optional. The distinctions mark register and formality.

sections.heading: Obligatory liaisons
sections.body:
Liaison is obligatory in these contexts:

1. Article + noun or adjective: les amis, un homme, des enfants.
2. Adjective + noun: petit ami, grand homme.
3. Pronoun + verb: nous avons, ils ont, vous êtes.
4. Preposition + article or pronoun: en été, chez eux, dans un.
5. Adverb + adjective: très intéressant, bien aimé.
6. Fixed expressions: de temps en temps, tout à fait.

In these cases, failure to make liaison is a mark of a non-native speaker.

sections.heading: Forbidden liaisons
sections.body:
Liaison is forbidden in these contexts:

1. After a singular noun: un garçon | intelligent (no liaison on the n of garçon).
2. Before an aspirated h: les | héros (no liaison).
3. After et: et | il vient (no liaison on the t).
4. Before the word 'oui': mais | oui (no liaison).
5. After an interrogative inversion where the verb ends in a nasal: comment | allez-vous (no liaison on the t of comment).

In these cases, making liaison is an error.

sections.heading: Optional liaisons
sections.body:
Between these, there are optional liaisons, which mark style. Making them sounds formal or literary. Omitting them sounds casual.

Example: 'pas encore' can be [paz‿ɑ̃kɔʁ] (formal) or [pa ɑ̃kɔʁ] (casual).

You will hear both in careful speech. In reading Racine or Molière aloud, you make the liaisons. In conversation, you pick and choose.

sections.heading: How liaison changes sounds
sections.body:
In liaison, the final consonant is not always pronounced as written:

- s and x → [z]: les amis [lez‿ami], deux ans [døz‿ɑ̃].
- d → [t]: grand homme [ɡʁɑ̃t‿ɔm].
- f → [v] in some fixed words: neuf ans [nœv‿ɑ̃], but neuf heures [nœf‿œʁ] (irregular).

The consonant that appears in liaison is the underlying form, preserved from Latin or Old French.

sections.heading: Listening drill
sections.instructions: Each phrase is read twice: once without liaison (where the next word starts with a consonant), once with liaison (where the next word starts with a vowel). Hear the difference.

items.answer: Linking a silent final consonant to the initial vowel of the next word.
Yes. Article + noun always requires liaison.
No. The h in 'héros' is aspirated, blocking liaison.

items.prompt: How is the s in 'les amis' pronounced?
How is the d in 'grand homme' pronounced in liaison?
What does it mean that some liaisons are optional?
items.answer: They are stylistic. Making them sounds formal; omitting them sounds casual.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 1.5 covers élision — dropping the final vowel before a word beginning with a vowel or mute h. The apostrophe as notation. Where liaison links consonants, élision drops vowels.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark complete when you can read ten short phrases aloud with correct obligatory liaisons.
